Due to its remoteness and short summer season, Mongolia has long been a destination overlooked by travelers.
But as the country moves to further open up to tourism by easing its entry conditions for international visitors and upgrading its infrastructure, 2023 might just be the best time yet to get there.
Here are 10 reasons travelers should start planning their long-dreamed-of Mongolia visit now.
With the government of Mongolia declaring 2023 through 2025 the “Years to Visit Mongolia,” citizens from an additional 34 countries can now visit the country visa-free through the end of 2025.
The addition of several European countries, including Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Norway, Spain, and the UK, as well as Australia and New Zealand, now brings the total number of countries and territories on the visa-exempt list to 61.
After years of delays, a pandemic and several controversies, the newly built Chinggis Khaan International Airport finally opened in the summer of 2021.
With the ability to handle approximately 3 million passengers a year (double that of the old airport), the addition of 500 new aircraft parking spaces and the infrastructure to support an increase in domestic as well as budget flights, the airport is a welcome addition to the country’s efforts to grow tourism.
Budget flights to Hong Kong from EZNIS Airways have been relaunched since the airport’s opening, and talks to resume direct flights to the United States are reportedly underway.
The recently opened Chinggis Khaan Museum offers a beautiful, fresh look at Mongolia’s tumultuous history.
With more than 10,000 artifacts spanning over 2,000 years, the museum explores the history of the Mongols and the empire they created – and eventually lost.
The museum’s artifacts are presented over eight floors, with six permanent and two temporary exhibition halls. Guided tours are offered in English every Saturday and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. free of charge.
When most people think of Mongolia, music festivals and conservation-focused art installations in the heart of one of the world’s largest deserts are the last things to come to mind.
But that’s all changing thanks to festivals like Playtime , Spirit of Gobi , INTRO Electronic Music Festival and the Kharkhorum 360 Visual Art & Music Experience .
Placing international bands, DJs, and musicians from around the world alongside Mongolia’s eclectic mix of rappers, bands and folk singers, the country just might be one of the world’s most underrated places for festival lovers.
The annual Naadam event has always been a great reason to visit Mongolia, but now that the festival has just celebrated its 100 year anniversary, 2023 is as good a time as ever to attend.
While the festival’s origins are rooted in the days of Genghis Khan, when he used horse racing, wrestling and archery competitions to keep his warriors in shape between battles, Naadam only officially became a national holiday 100 years ago.
Today, the festival – held in Ulaanbaatar at the National Sports Stadium, has a few more bells and whistles than it did during the days of the Great Khan.
A seat at July 11’s opening ceremony is always one of the hardest tickets to score in town.
Mounted archery is seeing a resurgence in Mongolia thanks to guys like Altankhuyag Nergui, one of the most accomplished archers in the sport and his archery academy, Namnaa .
Here, locals learn the fundamentals of Mongolian archery before mounting a horse and taking their new found skills to another level.
In the summer months, students and academy members put on weekly shows for interested spectators. The academy also offers day-long training sessions for those wanting to try this intense sport.
Speaking of giving life to Mongolia’s most ancient traditions, the resurrection of Mongol bichig, or the traditional Mongolian script written from top to bottom and read from left to right, has also seen a major resurgence in recent years.
Visit the Erdenesiin Khuree Mongolian Calligraphy Center in Karakorum to learn from master calligraphist Tamir Samandbadraa Purev about this important cultural heritage. And, while you’re there, browse the yurts filled with Tamir’s works.
Pair the release of Husqvarna’s new Norden 901 Expedition motorbike with Nomadic Off-Road’s newly announced Eagle Hunter Tour , and you have one of the fastest adventures in Mongolia.
The tour takes six riders 1,700 kilometers from Ulaanbaatar to Bayan-Ulgii, where riders eventually meet their hosts, Mongolia’s famous eagle hunters.
The only thing faster than this adventure is the rate at which Nomadic Off-Road’s tours sell out.
Capturing the art of the last eagle hunters of Mongolia
Professional musher Joel Rauzy has been leading dogsledding tours across the frozen Lake Khuvsgul for 18 years.
With fewer crowds, lower hotel rates and the chance to see one of the largest freshwater lakes in the world completely frozen over, winter in Mongolia is something else to see and experience.
Rauzy’s company, Wind of Mongolia , offers tours of the lake, where each person is assigned their own sled and dogs for the journey. Following Rauzy’s lead, mushers will make a loop of the lake. Activities include ice fishing, while travelers stay in winterized yurts and spend time with nomadic families along the journey.
Nestled in the heart of Selenge province on the Yeruu River, Yeruu Lodge is the brainchild of Norwegian founder Eirik Gulsrud Johnsen, who first visited Mongolia in 2017.
With a minimal Scandinavian-style restaurant and dining area, a handful of fully kitted out yurts for guests to stay in, two pétanque courts, kayaks, a driving range, mountain bikes and a yoga area, the lodge is a destination for nature lovers.
Completely off-grid, the lodge runs off solar panels, uses of thermal heating, and all of the property’s water comes from an on-property well and is recycled after use.
Additionally, all glass, metal and plastic used at the lodge is also recycled, and food waste is turned into compost used to grow vegetables, berries and herbs onsite.
The lodge is set to open in April 2023.

articles.title_zh: Why Caitlin Clark was at the center of a Hawks-Hawkeyes mix-up during Senate argument - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Special counsel Jack Smith, who brought two indictments against now-President Donald Trump in 2023, testified in front of Congress again on Tuesday — this time, to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Smith’s testimony comes as Republicans continue to probe the investigations into Trump and as some in the party, including the president, have pushed for often-unspecified criminal charges to be brought against Smith.
Here are the major takeaways from Tuesday’s hearing.
Republicans have struggled mightily to substantiate Trump’s desire for Smith to be charged criminally . But rarely has it seemed to backfire like it did Tuesday .
Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri crafted an apparent conspiracy theory about Smith being tied to the prosecution of Trump in Fulton County, Georgia. To substantiate his theory, Schmitt cited text messages he suggested showed Smith had been at an Atlanta Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Fulton County prosecutor Fani Willis and special prosecutor Nathan Wade admitted to an affair.
Smith appeared dumbfounded, though. He denied going to a Hawks game and said he had no recollection of even being in Atlanta.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warriors-Hawks game on February 3, 2024 – the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt said.
Schmitt went big on the allegation, telling Smith, “I don’t think you know that we have this stuff.” He urged Smith not to “perjure yourself.” He later called Smith a “dirtbag.” He later told the “Charlie Kirk Show” that he was just asking questions and seeing whether Smith would ensnare himself.
Eventually, Democrats got Schmitt to allow Smith to actually review the evidence – a poster featuring the texts in question. In one of them, a fellow prosecutor asks about a seat being reserved for Smith. The poster showed the Atlanta Hawks’ arena.
But by this point, Smith seemed to put it together. He said he was not at a game featuring the Atlanta Hawks , but rather the University of Iowa Hawkeyes women’s basketball team – which then featured Caitlin Clark – at the University of Maryland in the Washington, DC, area.
Smith’s recollection matches up with a game played that day.
Behind the scenes, a source familiar with how Schmitt got it wrong told CNN the Republican senator checked what men’s college and NBA games were scheduled that day and found only the Atlanta Hawks set to play — but he failed to consider that Smith may have been at a women’s basketball game.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, after clearing up the matter, said Schmitt should apologize.
Instead, he laughed it off, telling CNN later Tuesday: “Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?”
The Republican defended his pointed line of questioning, saying, “That’s what these hearings are for. You ask questions, you get answers. You know, Jack Smith has perjured himself before, but if he says he’s at the game, maybe he’s a Caitlin Clark fan. We’ll accept that.”
At the hearing, he maintained that the texts “could have obviously been related to the prosecution” in Fulton County. He said he stood by calling Smith a “dirtbag.”
The scene epitomized how speculative and thinly constructed the GOP’s allegations about Smith, Trump’s foes and about the justice system being weaponized against Trump have been. Likewise, the GOP’s other major perjury allegation against Smith rests on a complete misreading of the evidence .
But rarely has this apparent fishing expedition been laid so bare. Schmitt seemed to firmly believe he had nailed Smith on something. But just minutes later, it seemed to fall apart – and rather spectacularly so.
Smith is a very careful witness. He often pauses noticeably before answering a question — in a way that can be a little jarring.
But he’s also made clear that he wants to fight back against the Trump administration’s weaponization of the justice system against people like him. And on Tuesday, he was a little more animated and open.
He punctuated his opening statement by saying, “Fear may be contagious; courage is as well.”
He also called it an “outrage” that people he worked with were “targeted illegally, lost their jobs illegally, and had their lives turned upside down by this Department of Justice.”
When asked about the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling conferring presidents with a large degree of immunity, Smith said it “can be very dangerous for the rule of law” for powerful people to benefit from such exceptions.
He also jousted with lawmakers a little more than he did before, rather than dryly reciting facts.
When GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas asked him whether he had any regrets, Smith said he regretted that “the people I worked with have been unfairly fired and vilified.”
When  Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina claimed Smith unfairly targeted the phone records of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, Smith told her that Lindsey Graham had investigated Trump’s underlying voter-fraud claims and found them to be false.
And he said he won’t be going away quietly.
“I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the president or others,” Smith said.
That exchange with Darline Graham was also significant when it comes to learning something new about the attempted prosecutions of Trump.
The reason: Smith said Lindsey Graham was likely to be a witness in the case.
“I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant,” Smith said. “He was not a target of our investigation. In fact, he likely would have been a witness in our case. Your brother investigated the claims that Donald Trump was making. He found them to be false.”
Lindsey Graham publicly broke with Trump on the Senate floor after January 6 (i.e. “ count me out ”) and appeared to be initially helpful to investigators probing the situation.
He later reconciled with Trump and assailed Smith’s investigation when he was among those whose phone records were wrapped up in the probe — and even pushed to get a financial payout for it.
Smith’s comments suggest Graham could have played at least some role in proving the charges against Trump.
The former special counsel seemed to make a point to repeatedly vouch for members of his former staff  who were fired by Trump’s Justice Department and, in some cases, were repeatedly invoked by name at Tuesday’s hearing.
Smith even called them “heroes.”
“My view: These people are heroes, and I believe our country does not recognize and pay enough attention to people like that,” he said. “I think if we did, the partisan things that we’re discussing today – a lot of that would go away.”
Smith also warned about what ousting people like that would portend for the country.
“If you drive those people out of public service, the institutions we rely on for justice, for protecting our country — those institutions are weakened,” Smith said.
When Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff of California talked about how Smith had been attacked, Smith said it was “much more important that the public servants who I work with – that we stop vilifying public servants.”
It’s been nearly a year since Trump appeared alongside then-Attorney General Pam Bondi and claimed Smith had committed crimes.
“Hopefully the Attorney General is looking at what he’s done,” Trump added eight months ago on social media.
There’s been little since then to suggest the Trump administration is able to provide him what he wants. And Tuesday’s hearing often felt like going through the motions more so than anything else.
Apart from Schmitt’s attempt at a gotcha, other Republican lawmakers generally mined territory already covered in the January House Judiciary Committee hearing .
Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri and others repeated an allegation from months ago that Smith perjured himself with his denials about seeking the contents of lawmakers’ communications. But Smith pointed to the holes in that previously debunked theory.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up
articles.content_orig:
Millions of taxpayer dollars have already been spent on President Donald Trump’s hagiographic ads, according to estimates by a leading political ad-tracking firm. And a total of $20 million has been allocated for the effort, which watchdog groups have deemed illegal.
The TV airtime for the three different Trump ads has cost at least $2.5 million to date, the ad-tracking firm AdImpact told CNN.
The actual cost of the taxpayer-funded ad campaign is even higher, but can’t be fully ascertained.
The money for these ads is coming from Customs and Border Protection, or CBP for short, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN.
Earlier this month, the White House Office of Management and Budget, led by Russell Vought, allocated $20 million to CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.)
Shortly after the $20 million was allocated, CBP contracted an advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., for a national media campaign in the same dollar amount. Days later, the ads began to appear on national television, two additional sources told CNN. LMD’s parent company, MarCom Group, did not respond to CNN’s request for comment.
CBP is an agency within the Department of Homeland Security. On Tuesday, two Democratic senators, Patty Murray and Chris Murphy, sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin accusing the department of “a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars.”
The propagandistic ads also faced a fresh challenge from the government watchdog group Public Citizen on Tuesday.
The ads “appear to violate the federal law against using taxpayer funds to finance propaganda and related provisions of the appropriations laws as well as the Hatch Act,” Public Citizen co-presidents Robert Weissman and Lisa Gilbert and the group’s lobbyist, Craig Holman, wrote in a complaint to the Federal Communications Commission and the Federal Trade Commission.
It’s unclear whether any outside groups have the legal standing to sue the Trump administration over the ads.
And while lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have questioned their legality, Republicans — who currently control both the House and the Senate — have not acted.
AdImpact’s analysis for CNN found 2,766 total ad airings between September 23 and 29. The ads have aired on Fox News and the big four broadcast networks.
About 30% of the ad spend has been dedicated to NFL and college football games, according to the firm’s research.
The ads have also appeared during shows like ABC’s “The View,” CBS’s “Elsbeth” and NBC’s “The Weakest Link.”
Because the spots have been classified as a “public service announcement” rather than a traditional political ad buy, the exact spending is not publicly disclosed or verifiable. AdImpact’s estimates are based on air dates, times, local markets, and other factors.
The firm said the first Trump ad to air, featuring the song “Love Me” by JMSN, has aired on more than 1,300 occasions so far.
Lawyers for JMSN sent a cease-and-desist letter to the White House earlier this week, demanding that the administration no longer use the song.
The text “Paid for by the US Government” is seen on screen at the end of each of the three ads, including one repurposed version of an ad from Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.
The “paid for” disclosure conflicts with the administration’s insistence that the ads are “public service announcements” akin to those that past administrations have aired about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccinations.
For actual public service announcements, the TV airtime is usually donated.
Public Citizen argued in its FCC and FTC complaint that the Trump ads “do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program.”
The ads were created in-house by the White House video team, two Trump advisers told CNN, and were personally driven by the president, who was involved in the selection of imagery and videos used, according to a separate source.
The Wall Street Journal first reported where the money came from.
On Tuesday, Public Citizen warned that TV stations could theoretically lose their broadcast licenses for knowingly airing the ads.
“A station knowingly broadcasting illegal, taxpayer-funded partisan propaganda has failed its public interest mandate, forming the basis of a formal license renewal challenge,” they wrote.
The track record of Trump’s FCC, however, shows the agency won’t try to penalize a station for running pro-Trump content. Instead, the agency has challenged ABC’s licenses, a move that many observers have linked to the network’s support for programs like “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” that are harshly critical of the president.
Public Citizen also filed a separate complaint Monday with the Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan agency typically tasked with investigating this type of issue, as well as the US Office of the Special Counsel, calling for an investigation “into who produced these ads and at what cost to taxpayers.”
What constitutes illegal government propaganda, and who can be held accountable for it, is less straightforward.
Propaganda hasn’t been defined in US law, but the Government Accountability Office has identified three categories, including “self-aggrandizement” or “puffery.”
“The most immediate check on this kind of behavior is supposed to be and needs to be Congress. Congress has not asserted itself as the first branch of government with the power of the purse to hold the president accountable,” said Donald Sherman, president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics, or CREW.
GOP lawmakers may be hesitant to provide accountability, he added, because the ads “are designed to boost Republicans in Congress.”
And Hatch Act violations — government officials engaging in partisan political activity while on duty — have largely been dismissed in recent years. Trump administration officials in his first term were alleged to have repeatedly violated the Hatch Act with no penalty. The same was alleged during the Biden administration.
Public Citizen said in a previous statement that it has filed dozens of complaints with the administration about Hatch Act violations, but thinks they have been ignored.

articles.title_orig: 2 Indians Charged In US For Selling Fake Ozempic. They Smuggled It From China
articles.title_zh: 2 Indians Charged In US For Selling Fake Ozempic. They Smuggled It From China
articles.content_orig:
Two Indian nationals have been charged in federal court in Florida with an alleged conspiracy to smuggle counterfeit Ozempic from China in a scheme that purportedly continued even after the Food and Drug Administration seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it, the Department of Justice said Tuesday.
One of the men, 33-year-old Swapnadip Roy, was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday.
Roy and his alleged co-conspirator, Vicky Ramancha, 37, are charged in an indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and to defraud the U.S., three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, they both face a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison.
Ramancha remains at large.
Court documents state Roy and Ramancha, starting in July 2023 and continuing to the following April, allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The popular drug is made by Novo , which recently rebranded from its name Novo Nordisk.
The material they and their co-conspirators allegedly distributed "included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers into believing they were purchasing authentic Ozempic authorized by the manufacturer," DOJ said.
The newly unsealed indictment says that in July 2023, Ramancha executed a sales and purchase agreement with an unidentified company in Lakeland, Florida, agreeing to supply that company with a product described as being Ozempic "at deeply discounted pricing."
A month later, Ramancha executed another agreement with a company in Sanford, Florida, to supply it with a product described as "Ozempic syringes" at deeply discounted pricing, the indictment alleges.
in November 2023, "Roy utilized threats to facilitate the distribution of product in the United States," writing, "Listen i am not your friend okay? I am not that guy," the indictment alleges.
Roy continued, "I am the guy that will cut some one [expletive] head off and [expletive] peoples dead wives corpse with it," the indictment alleges. "You [expletive] up Solve the [expletive] problem. Get the truck over there today."
After Roy and Ramancha learned that the FDA had seized some of their product that they had distributed in the U.S., a co-conspirator asked Ramancha whether the related FDA warning would affect a pending order to 60,000 additional units of Ozempic, the indictment says.
"Ramancha replied, 'Not at all. But you have to make sure your client are not being idiotic,'" the indictment alleges.
The case comes as the use of so-called GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic for weight loss has become increasingly popular in the U.S.
In July, Gallup reported that the percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes rose to 11% in  2026, compared to 3% in 2024.
"And 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, an increase of nine percentage points" over 2024, Gallup noted.
"Counterfeit prescription drugs — especially common ones — threaten the health and safety of every American who depends on the integrity of our pharmaceutical supply," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said in a statement Tuesday.
"These defendants allegedly exploited people's health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs," Duva said.

articles.title_orig: Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
articles.title_zh: Trump announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI deal among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

articles.title_orig: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.title_zh: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022
The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank , including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children.
The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor.
Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee.
“While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”
Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad.
Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen.
The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him.
Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it.
“If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.”
In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank.
The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025.
A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Many of the Democrats , who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years.
When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs.
The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

articles.title_orig: California bans officers’ use of electric-shock gloves after ICE reveals plan to equip agents
articles.title_zh: California bans officers’ use of electric-shock gloves after ICE reveals plan to equip agents
articles.content_orig:
State passes law banning local, state and federal officers from using gloves that deliver painful electric shocks
California has passed a law Tuesday banning local, state and federal law enforcement officers from using gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to people .
The ban on shock gloves will take effect next year and remain in place until 2030. It comes weeks after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) moved to equip its officers with the gloves, which are designed to gain compliance from combative individuals. Last month, the agency awarded a nearly $17m contract to buy 6,000 pairs.
“Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, said in a statement after signing the law. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state.”
The law is the latest example of how Democratic-led states have been pushing back against Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts since he took office last year. In California, lawmakers passed at least two dozen bills this year seeking to fortify immigrants’ rights, restrict cooperation with federal immigration agents and tighten regulations on immigrant detention facilities, among other things.
Nationwide, 17 states with Democratic-led legislatures have passed a total of more than 100 pro-immigrant bills this year, according to an Associated Press analysis using the bill tracking software Plural. The most common purpose is to limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement agents.
LaShae Sharp-Collins, a Democratic California assembly member, said she introduced the shock-gloves legislation to “put a pause” on law enforcement’s use of the devices while the state examines their potential risks. The law requires the state’s justice department to study their safety and report to lawmakers by 2029.
“There’s a lot of unrest and a lot of uncertainty,” she said in an interview. “A lot of people are scared.”
The law will again test the state’s authority to restrict federal agents amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. A federal judge earlier this year blocked the state’s first-in-the-nation law barring federal officers from wearing face coverings, deeming it too selective because it applied to local and federal law enforcement but exempted state officers.
Lawmakers passed a new bill this year to make the ban apply to all officers. Newsom signed that legislation.
Kevin Johnson, a professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis School of Law, said courts are likely to ultimately rule that the state cannot bar federal officers from wearing shock gloves or face coverings. The laws are well-intentioned, he said, but likely conflict with the supremacy clause of the US constitution, which generally sets federal law as supreme over conflicting state law.
“The state has very limited, if any, powers in dictating to the federal government how its officers are armed,” he said.
Sacramento sheriff Jim Cooper, a Democrat and former state lawmaker, said banning shock gloves “really makes no sense” because they are among the non-lethal tools officers can use if necessary.
“When the federal government does something, the state legislature wants to ban it,” he said at a news conference. “They’re making our job harder.”
Sharp-Collins said ICE’s plan to use shock gloves was the catalyst for the ban. But she cited their use by other officers, including a case in which a Kentucky family alleged a man died after being tased and shocked with the gloves dozens of times while in law enforcement custody in 2024.
Scott Wiener, a state senator and San Francisco Democrat who wrote last year’s mask ban, also authored this year’s measure to expand it to state officers.
“California must use every available tool to stand up for our communities under attack from ICE’s secret police terror campaign,” he said in a statement after it passed the legislature.

articles.title_orig: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.title_zh: Caleb Flynn found guilty on all charges in wife's death
articles.content_orig:
Caleb Flynn, the former pastor and "American Idol" contestant, has been found guilty on all charges in the killing of his wife.
Flynn's wife Ashley was found dead in their Tipp City home in February.
A jury found Flynn guilty on all charges and gun specifications: aggravated murder, three counts of murder, two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence.
Watch the verdict as it's read here
The jury deliberated for a little over two hours before returning a verdict.
Sentencing has been set for Oct. 5 at 3 p.m.
" We're disappointed. I fully anticipate a notice of appeal filed," Defense Attorney Patrick Mulligan said, saying he anticipates the decision will be "fully tested."
Mulligan said they will file an appeal of the verdict on the basis of lack of sufficient evidence.
When asked about Caleb's reaction, Mulligan said "he was upset."
When asked if they would have done anything differently, Mulligan replied no.
In the hours after the trial concluded, prosecutors in the case thanked Ashley’s family for their trust in law enforcement and in the process.
Prosecutors also read a statement from Ashley’s family, which said the verdict brought justice and accountability, but added that no verdict will be able to bring her back for her loved ones.
The following statement was read by Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins on behalf of Ashley's family:
"Today's verdict brings justice and accountability for Ashley's death, and our family is deeply grateful to everyone who helped bring us to this moment.
However, no verdict can bring Ashley back, give the girls back their mother, or erase the pain our family has endured. The cruelty of what happened to Ashley—and the things we have been forced to hear and relive—has at times felt unbearable.
But through all of it, we've held tightly to this truth: Ashley's life will not be defined by the way it ended. She'll be remembered for the way she lived.
Ashley loved Jesus with her whole heart. Her faith wasn't something she simply spoke about; it was how she lived. She loved people well, found joy beyond her circumstances, prayed boldly for her family, and wanted her life to point people to Jesus.
Most of all, she loved being a mom. She prayed over her girls, taught them to love God, and showed them what it looked like to live with faith, kindness, joy, and grace.
We refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley's life have the final word in her story. Our faith does not erase our grief, but it carries us through it. We know Ashley is home with the Lord she loved and served.
As this chapter closes, our prayer is that Ashley's story does not end with a verdict. We pray that it continues through her girls, our family, and every person touched by the way she lived.
If you want to honor Ashley, love people well. Pray boldly for your family. Choose joy, and point people to Jesus.
We are deeply grateful to the jury for its care and service; the Miami County Prosecutor's Office; the Tipp City Police Department; the FBI; BCI; and every investigator and advocate who worked tirelessly to seek the truth.
Thank you to everyone who has prayed for, loved, and supported our family. We ask for privacy now as we continue healing and loving Ashley's girls the way she would want them to be loved.
Please remember Ashley not for how she died, but for how beautifully she lived."

During closings, the prosecution broke down the charges Caleb is facing, discussed what the state must prove, described a potential motive, Flynn's cell phone activity, asking the jury to find him guilty on all counts.
The defense challenged the evidence presented and Flynn's former mistress Alleigha Botner's testimony.
Mulligan claimed Flynn's affair does not equal a murder, while questioning Botner's actions and motive.
The judge then read lengthy jury instructions before the jury went into the deliberation room. The bailiff did note the jury received lunch first, so deliberations didn't likely begin until around 1:15 p.m.
During the trial, the state called dozens of witnesses, from special agents to experts to family members.
The defense did not call a single witness.
Jurors heard most from Flynn's former mistress, Alleigha Botner, who took the stand for two days and read dozens of the more than 100,000 text messages that the two exchanged
Prosecutors say Flynn and Botner exchanged more than 107,000 messages. On the stand, Botner read messages spanning months in which both expressed hatred toward Ashley and discussed a future together.
At one point, Botner became emotional while reading a July exchange.
“I just wish I didn’t say this,” Botner said before telling the jury she had written, “I want to kill her, Caleb.”
When a prosecutor asked who sent that message, Botner answered, “Me.”
Flynn responded, according to Botner, “That makes two of us.”
Botner testified that the couple often referred to Ashley using an insulting nickname. In one message, Flynn allegedly wrote that Ashley had “ruined and taken everything” from him and that he could not stand the sight or mention of her.
The messages also showed Botner repeatedly pressuring Flynn to leave his wife. She set several deadlines, at times threatening to end their relationship if he did not follow through.
The state also called investigators and members of Ashley's family to the stand, all providing different pieces of evidence for their case.
While no witnesses were called, the defense did spend time on the last day of testimony emphasizing missing physical evidence, challenging the lead investigator about evidence that was either not found or not collected.
Detective Sgt. Mike Morgan acknowledged that investigators did not find Ashley’s blood on Flynn or his clothing. He also testified that investigators did not obtain results from blood-spatter evidence and never recovered the gun used in the shooting.
Morgan confirmed that Flynn was not tested for gunshot residue.
“There was never a gunshot residue test done in this particular case, correct?” a defense attorney asked.
“Correct,” Morgan responded.

By Nellie Andreeva , Peter White
One of the biggest executive suite questions about Paramount following its pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery — who will lead streaming — has been answered.
Cindy Holland is leaving Paramount Skydance where she was Chair of Direct-To-Consumer having previously served as an advisor to Skydance CEO David Ellison. Her last day is today. Holland announced her departure in a company memo, which you can read below.
The move, which had been rumored for the past week, leaves Casey Bloys, Chairman and CEO of HBO and HBO Max Content, as the presumed streaming head of the combined Paramount-WBD. Holland hinted at that in her email to staff, indicating that Ellison had shared with her his plan for the leadership of the combined HBO Max and Paramount+ streamer, and it involved him “optimizing for HBO stability” (aka going with Bloys), something Holland supported.
Since Ellison announced earlier this year that HBO Max and Paramount+ will merge into one streaming platform after Paramount’s acquisition of WBD, it has become clear that the move would come down to a choice between Holland and Bloys for who would lead the combined streaming operation as both are accomplished top-level streaming executives, neither of whom would report to the other.
“As David readies for the next phase of his vision, we’ve discussed my role and the future of the combined businesses. David is optimizing for HBO stability as we move into this next chapter, and I fully support that,” Holland wrote. “I know this team has the leadership and expertise to manage through the transition and the next phase of the company, and to this end today will mark my last day here.”
Holland, who was behind Netflix’s foray into original programming , was initially recruited by Ellison as an advisor to help draft the post-Paramount merger streaming strategy before she took the rains of the operation as Chair of Direct-to-Consumer of Paramount Skydance in August 2025, overseeing Paramount+ and Pluto.
“Cindy is one of the most exceptional executives in our industry — a force of nature whose impact on Paramount over the past year has been significant,” Paramount CEO Ellison said. “Under her leadership, P+ reached new heights, Pluto TV underwent its most significant transformation in a decade, and we strengthened our content and sports portfolio – all while the business exceeded the ambitious goals we set. Just as importantly, she built an exceptional team and a strong foundation for the future. Cindy has been a trusted partner to me and so many others, and I couldn’t be more grateful for her leadership, her relentless drive and everything she’s done for our company.”
Holland’s departure raises questions about the post-merger future of her top executives, some of whom have been longtime close collaborators of hers, led by Paramount+ Head of Originals Jane Wiseman, who worked for Holland at Netflix and Sister before joining her at Paramount.
The two put together Paramount+’s programming strategy, which includes expanding the slate, dominated by Taylor Sheridan dramas into “female forward dramas” with a string of series orders, starting with Discretion , starring Nicole Kidman, which recently began production.
Bloys had indicated that he would like to keep his senior HBO team intact after parent WBD is acquired by Paramount.
In her note, Holland reflected on some of her accomplishments over the past 13 months.
“We grew Paramount+ to an all-time subscriber high, delivered the best retention in the service’s history, and drove double-digit growth in both engagement and revenue,” she said. “We built an extraordinary content pipeline, greenlighting more than 40 new and returning series and setting all-time records with Landman , the most-watched series in Paramount+ history, and Dutton Ranch, the service’s biggest original series debut ever.”
During her tenure, Sheridan, who is behind Paramount+’s biggest hits, including Landman, Dutton Ranch, Lioness and Tulsa King , announced that he would be moving to NBCUniversal in January 2029. Meanwhile, Holland played a key role in attracting Stranger Things creators the Duffer Brothers, whose show she had championed at Netflix, for a big film and TV overall deal at Paramount.
Holland’s memo indicates that WBD may have been a target for Ellison months before he made the first unsolicited offer for the company in September 2025 while his Skydance Media was still going through regulatory approval on its Paramount acquisition.
“When I joined David’s team in January 2025, we proceeded to set three goals: i) advise on the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, ii) integrate and transform Paramount+ & revive Pluto TV, and iii) build an unparalleled team in this industry,” Holland said. “In just over 12 months, I’m proud to say we accomplished all three and it’s been a joy to work closely with all of you.”
She also gave the WBD merger her full endorsement.
“I joined Paramount because I believe in these businesses, and because I believe wholeheartedly that the combination of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery serves the best interests of artists and audiences worldwide,” Holland said. “I’m looking forward to seeing what you all accomplish together in this next, momentous chapter.”
During her nearly two decades at Netflix, including nine years as VP Original Content, Holland established the streamer’s original programing strategy and spearheaded the crop of scripted series that put the streamer on the map, including House of Cards, Orange Is the New Black, BoJack Horseman , The Crown and The Queen’s Gambit.
Since her departure from the streamer in September 2020, Holland had taken on board and advisory roles before returning to the executive ranks as Global CEO of Elisabeth Murdoch and Jane Featherstone‘s Sister in 2023. She spent 15 months in the role before taking the Senior Advisor position at Skydance.

articles.title_zh: One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford called 999 himself
articles.content_orig:
One of five men arrested near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday morning had dialled 999 himself, the BBC understands.
The suspect called the police at 00:45 BST, almost an hour before a farmer also dialled 999 after seeing men in balaclavas.
The five were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after three vans were spotted, sparking a major security incident around the Gloucestershire base which the US military operates.
They were released on bail on Monday in what police described as an "investigative decision" "grounded in experience and strategy".
Police say a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the vans.
Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by the farmer.
She told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men".
"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.
In the latest development -  first reported by the Times newspaper - it is claimed the suspect called police almost an hour before a local farmer also raised the alarm.
A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.
But Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning had been due to "a range of information".
Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.
The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.
Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation.
"The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday.
"I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."
The RAF base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told journalists he was "disappointed" the five men had been released on bail.
Taylor has said officers are exploring "multiple lines of inquiry", including whether proxies or individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state were involved.
In an update on Tuesday, he added that the incident had been worrying for many people, with this "heightened by the international commentary that we are seeing" in an apparent reference to comments from the US administration.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting on Monday afternoon and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts".
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
However, the Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the latest incident.

articles.title_orig: Jane Doe in Cornell University case told campus police, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," transcript shows
articles.title_zh: Jane Doe in Cornell University case told campus police, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," transcript shows
articles.content_orig:
We're getting new insight into how Cornell University Police handled the case of an alleged fraternity gang rape back in 2024.
Cornell conducted an internal investigation that led to expulsions, suspensions and other sanctions. The response by law enforcement has come under new scrutiny, and prosecutors have now reopened their criminal investigation .
CBS News New York investigative reporter Mahsa Saeidi exclusively obtained a transcript of the alleged victim's interview with campus police from a source.
The interview began on Nov. 14 — more than three weeks after the alleged gang rape — and continued the next day.
A campus police investigator led the questioning. A Title IX investigator, a victim advocate, and Jane Doe's adviser were also in the room for the first day of the interview.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe described drinking and using drugs the night of the alleged rape, and said she had gaps in her memory.
The transcript shows she distinguished the initial sexual activity from what she says happened later, and when asked whether she was OK with the initial encounter, she said, "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this."
Jane Doe added, according to the transcript, "And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard."
When describing what happened later in the night, the transcript says Jane Doe said, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
The transcript shows that throughout the interview, the investigator asks questions as he prepares her written statement.
He typed up her account, read it back word by word, and gave her a chance to clarify or correct the record.
On the second day of the interview, Jane Doe reviewed the revised six-page statement. The transcript shows her adviser asked if she wants her and another adviser to review the statement.
Before signing, the transcript shows Jane Doe said, "I'm very confident about this."
The Tompkins County District Attorney says Jane Doe's signed 2024 statement was central to his decision not to bring charges.
CBS News New York has not seen Jane Doe's final six-page statement. CBS News New York did reach out to her attorney and Cornell, and has not heard back yet.
Previously, Jane Doe's attorney said his client was in denial after the alleged attack.
CBS News New York is in touch with attorneys for two defendants named in the lawsuit, and they say their clients deny the charges.
CBS News New York will have more on this developing story later this evening.

Xbox’s disc-to-digital feature has been in testing for insiders for about a month now , and the momentum is picking up. Ubisoft joined the program not long ago , and SEGA has now seemingly followed suit.
Beyond the new publisher participation, there have been some tweaks to how the feature actually works. So, let’s go over what’s changed.
If you’ve been living under a rock and aren’t sure what this fabled feature is, I’ll quickly explain. Disc-to-digital allows you to insert participating discs into your Xbox One or Series X console to obtain a digital license. Once you have that license, you can keep playing the game without the disc even being inserted. It also unlocks access to the game on other platforms if it’s a Play Anywhere title, as well as through cloud gaming .
With that out of the way, how exactly is the experience changing? The digital entitlement is now granted automatically when you insert a disc, rather than requiring a manual step from the menu. Additionally, the service will only provide a full-screen explanation on your first digital entitlement. For any subsequent games, you’ll just see a simple toast notification.
Perhaps the biggest update, however, is that fans have started noticing select SEGA games allowing digital entitlement. Titles like Persona 5 Royal are already in. If all SEGA games work out similarly, that would add another 44 games to the program.
For those keeping count, or if you follow @XCTdotLIVE on X (formerly Twitter), that brings the current disc-to-digital count to 1,585 games , with 205 games currently not in the service. Considering the feature is still in testing, I’m personally expecting that figure to grow, especially as more publishers get on board.
Currently, publishers who aren’t participating include Bandai Namco and Square Enix . While I can’t speak much for Bandai Namco, I do presume that, given Square’s fondness for Xbox as of late, we’ll at the very least see them get on board at some stage.
Xbox’s disc-to-digital feature continues to impress. At least, I’m impressed anyway; in fact, it even got me buying physical games again. It’s a bit of a shame to think we could have had such a forward-thinking feature as far back as the Xbox One, but I digress.
Let me know your thoughts on disc-to-digital, what games you want to see enter the service that haven’t already, and anything else that comes to mind in the comments.

articles.title_orig: US Supreme Court denies Christa Pike's last-ditch bid to halt execution
articles.title_zh: US Supreme Court denies Christa Pike's last-ditch bid to halt execution
articles.content_orig:
The US Supreme Court has declined to stop the execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike on the eve of the date appointed for her death by lethal injection.
Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of a teenage classmate.
Hoping for a last-minute reprieve, her attorneys filed a petition with the high court ahead of her scheduled execution on Wednesday morning.
But after the high court's decision to deny that request, Pike will be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.
On Monday, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee denied a request for clemency from Pike, saying he would not intervene in her planned execution.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Slemmer's murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself.
She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.
Her attorneys have argued that "an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain" and that Pike was too young at the time of the murder to be sentenced to death for it.
At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.
She is due to be executed at 11:00 EDT (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
Additional reporting from Sareen Habeshian.
Clarification 29 September: This article originally referred to a pentagram as "a symbol of Satanic ritual". We have amended the wording to make clear that the symbol in question was an inverted pentagram and to clarify that such symbols are associated with some satanic groups. The article has been updated accordingly.

articles.title_zh: Trump and major AI executives sign "morally binding" voluntary controls: "It's almost like a constitution"
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

articles.title_zh: GOP senator airballs perjury claim against Jack Smith over apparent Hawks/Hawkeyes mix-up
articles.content_orig:
His slam dunk was a brick.
Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., accused former special counsel Jack Smith on Tuesday of committing perjury when he denied having attended a specific Atlanta Hawks basketball game in 2024 — to Smith’s apparent confusion.
The attempted trick play happened during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Smith’s now-scuttled investigations into President Donald Trump. But it soon emerged that Schmitt had the wrong team.
“Did you go to an NBA game between the Golden State Warriors and the Atlanta Hawks on Feb. 3, 2024?” Schmitt asked.
“What city would that be in?” a confused-looking Smith replied.
“Atlanta,” Schmitt responded.
Schmitt pressed him again about whether he was in Atlanta on that date and then said he’d give him some “context” — it was the day after Fani Willis , the district attorney of Fulton County, Georgia, “came clean” about her romantic relationship with a prosecutor in her then-pending criminal case against Trump.
“The next day were you in Atlanta?” Schmitt continued.
“I do not believe so,” Smith responded. “I definitely did not go to a Hawks game. I’m sure of that.”
Schmitt then asked whether he ever met with the local prosecutors in Atlanta who charged Trump. “No,” Smith said.
“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta, at a Warrior-Hawks game, on Feb. 3, 2024, the day after Willis and [Nathan] Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt continued as a staffer held up a poster board that had three text messages about Smith’s going to an event.
The staffer quickly took the poster down as Smith looked on, appearing confused.
“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t perjure yourself,” Schmitt said.
Smith complained that it had been taken down too quickly and that he hadn’t gotten to look at it. “I think you’ve already perjured yourself,” Schmitt told him, adding later that he’d go down in history as “a total dirtbag.”
Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who was next in line to question Smith, gave him an opportunity to further respond to Schmitt’s attack.
Smith said the only game he remembered going to around that time was a University of Maryland basketball game against the Iowa Hawkeyes featuring star player Caitlin Clark. “The Marshals Service was there with me. You could check if that was the exact date,” Smith said.
Klobuchar then checked the date of the Maryland-Iowa game.
“We have confirmed that, in fact, you are right, Mr. Smith. Iowa, the Iowa Hawkeyes, played Maryland on Feb. 3, 2024. The final score was 93-85. Iowa won, and Caitlin Clark scored over, scored 30 points,” and the game was in Maryland, she said.
She also chided Schmitt for appearing to mix up the Hawks and the Hawkeyes.
“I would just say for a U.S. senator to have false information and imply based on a confusion about the name of a team, which I knew, knowing my Midwestern sports, and imply that you were in another city, that you were somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a dirtbag is something that deserves an apology,” Klobuchar said.
Schmitt didn’t apologize. Asked by NBC News afterward whether he still thought Smith had perjured himself, he said: “We’ll find out. That’s going to be up to a prosecutor to determine. My job here today was to ask questions and get answers.”
Despite the flub, some right-wing commentators and outlets praised Schmitt for the exchange. Pro-Trump influencer Benny Johnson posted on X that Schmitt “CAUGHT Jack Smith perjuring himself” and “pulled out the receipts.” The post appeared to have been taken down by the late afternoon.
Schmitt later went on “ The Charlie Kirk Show ,” where one of the hosts praised him for the “great moment.” “Good for you on that,” host Andrew Kolvet said.
“Gotta give you some flowers for that, sir,” he said, saying Smith “sat there acting dumbfounded and completely clueless.”
“It was the only NBA or NCAA men’s game going on at that time in Atlanta. He claimed later that he was at another game,” Schmitt responded. “Here’s the thing — my job is to ask the questions. If that’s what his answer is, that’s what his answer is.”
On Tuesday night, Schmitt wrote in a post on X , “Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?”
Rebecca Shabad is a politics reporter for NBC News based in Washington.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI takes on Meta with dots agent in autonomous AI push
articles.title_zh: OpenAI takes on Meta with dots agent in autonomous AI push
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO — Leading AI company OpenAI tried to navigate through a storm of controversy on a cloudless San Francisco Tuesday, touting a new wave of products and tools it said would empower users with autonomous assistants.
Welcoming around 2,500 software engineers and AI aficionados on an oceanside pier for the company’s biggest-ever celebration of technical developers, OpenAI released several new products while holding back its most advanced system for safety reasons.
CEO Sam Altman kicked off the day by unveiling Dots — autonomous AI systems, or AI agents, that function continuously to carry out tasks on behalf of users.
“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, proclaiming that Dots allowed him to delegate tasks and regain some of his attention for other meaningful tasks. “I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way. It’s the way I’ve always wanted to work with AI,” he said.
OpenAI said Dots can accomplish “nearly anything” using their own cloud computer, web browser and connections to the over 4,000 applications that already function with ChatGPT, such as Slack or Google Drive.
Hit by a Silicon Valley spell of Murphy’s Law, the opening keynote was beset by a series of technical difficulties.
Romain Huet, head of developer experience at OpenAI, ran into trouble trying to showcase users’ ability to direct Dots by voice commands. “Voice chat couldn’t start,” the mainstage display beamed out to the audience.
“I think maybe Dottie is having kind of a slow morning,” said Holly Li, who helps lead OpenAI’s product team, referring to her Dot assistant after it didn’t answer one of her live requests to update her on a team’s progress. Despite the live hiccup, Li said Dots had already changed how OpenAI staffers accomplish their work.
“People started treating their Dots like their delegates, and now we bring our Dots into group chats from the get-go,” she said during the morning keynote session.
The day featured a series of events and technical demonstrations, allowing users to hear from industry experts about new pricing models and agentic setups, while about 50 protesters railed against the company’s military and government contracts outside the facility.
“People over billionaires,” proclaimed a bright orange banner as people entered the oceanside facility to learn about fuzzy orange Dots.
Questions of trust and safety hovered over the event. The evening before the new products were launched, OpenAI apologized for its agents’ hacking of an Australian government website. “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” it said in a blog post .
The incident, which occurred in June, involved an internal model under development, which accessed nonpublic information related to Australia’s public health insurance program. On Tuesday, Altman and OpenAI leadership stressed that the episode — and other major incidents of OpenAI’s systems’ going rogue or acting in unintended ways — all involved models that were not meant for public release and were distinct from the commercial offerings available to users.
“The instances we disclosed were running internal-only models that were not on track to ship,” said Alex Embericos, a product lead at OpenAI.
Despite the distinction, Altman said there is a trade-off between pushing the frontier of AI development and building cutting-edge AI systems safely.
“To push models to the new level of capability, it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety and security stay well ahead of capabilities,” he told reporters after his keynote speech. “But you can see that we were able to build a huge amount of useful new stuff without a major new model, and there will be new models.”
On Monday, OpenAI announced that it would refrain from releasing its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because of concerns that the system did not follow human instructions. “While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization,” head of safety systems Saachi Jain said in a statement.
OpenAI’s leaders also acknowledged that its new products would require significant computational resources, with Altman classifying Dots as a “premium product.” He said the company hopes to eventually roll out a version of Dots to a mass-market audience in the future, citing the computational intensity as a reason for the phased debut.
Dots are available only for users who subscribe to OpenAI’s Pro offering, which costs $100 to $500 a month, as well as Business Premium and some Enterprise users. Dots are also unavailable in Europe and the United Kingdom, which Altman chalked up to the region’s strict regulations.
“We have a great track record of getting our stuff launched in the E.U., but they do have a process that takes longer, and sometimes unpredictably longer,” Altman told NBC News. “But we really want to ship all of our stuff to Europeans.”
Altman unveiled Dots weeks after Facebook and Instagram maker Meta released its Muse series of AI agents, which it bills as “your personal agent.” The Muse app has shot to the top spot on both the Apple and Android app stores, quickly outpacing the Grok Bot agentic AI offering from Elon Musk’s xAI.
OpenAI also unveiled a new model , GPT-6.1 Sol, that it said nearly matches its top-line Astra model in terms of performance for a fraction of the price, in addition to announcing beefed-up privacy protocols and a new collaborative space for users to engage with its systems — aptly called “ChatGPT Space.”
While Altman and OpenAI employees were promoting their new offerings, across the country OpenAI President Greg Brockman was meeting with President Donald Trump and dozens of other tech leaders to chart out an ambitious view of AI. Trump used the opportunity to “inaugurate the era of super intelligence.”
Altman said he hoped the Washington meeting allowed AI titans to forge consensus on risks from AI while allowing society to embrace the technology’s potential upsides.
Altman said he disagreed with industry leaders who refused to acknowledge that AI could pose significant risks — “you can imagine a legitimate loss-of-control accident to an AI because we do not take safety and security seriously enough” — while distancing himself from claims that AI could kill all of humanity within a few years.
“My hope is that in this industry we can come together and say we need to get down this middle path between those two,” he said.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.
