articles.title_zh: Carney accuses US steelmaker of betraying Canadian workers after layoffs tied to Trump tariffs
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton are facing an uncertain future after the company announced Monday it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.
Ron Wells, the president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, says the wind-down is expected to begin Oct. 9, with about 350 workers from the Hamilton plant expected to be laid off.
He said the total layoffs could be up to 500 in total, between the Hamilton and Lake Erie Works plant in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has also said up to 500 workers could be affected.
"I hate using 'we're disappointed' — we're disgusted," Wells told CBC Hamilton Tuesday morning.
Hamilton steel plant to lay off hundreds of workers as U.S. tariffs prompt 'survival' move
For families connected to the plant, the uncertainty is already taking a toll.
Jillian Watt's husband is a line worker, and has worked at Stelco in Hamilton for 21 years. She said he has not yet been told whether he will be among those laid off.
"They haven't spoken to individuals, so it's kind of still up in the air," she said Tuesday morning. Watt, who is a union representative for a Canadian Union of Public Employees heath workers local, spoke to CBC from the entrance to National Steel Car, just down the road from Stelco.
National Steel Car workers have been on strike for a 48 days and have been regularly joined on the picket line by other unionized workers.
Watt is particularly concerned about whether her husband's experience with the company is enough if layoffs are decided by seniority. She said the possibility of losing the family's main source of income is particularly stressful.
"He's a breadwinner for our family. We have four kids, you know, trying to make it by," she said. "It was a bit of a kick to the gut for both of us."
Watt said her husband had already been concerned about the plant in recent months, as operations were idled and orders slowed. Now, they are awaiting the verdict of what happens next. "It's very stressful," she said.
Wells said the union was told about the layoffs during a meeting with the company Monday morning.
He said he has been talking with workers concerned about how long the layoffs could last because the company has not provided an end date.
"They're asking how long is this going to last? Should we start looking for another job?" Wells said. "People are concerned."
The company has said some affected workers could be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.
But Wells said the union was told there are only roughly 40 to 45 openings there — a number he says falls well short of the potential layoffs in Hamilton.
Wells is also questioning the commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.
He said the agreement included a commitment to maintain the number of unionized employees for five years, and he wants the federal government to enforce it.
"You have people making these decisions in Cleveland and they have no ties to our community," Well said. "If 350 Hamiltonians lose their jobs, they don't care."
Hamilton steelmaker Stelco sold to Cleveland-Cliffs for $3.4B
Pat Persico, the senior director of corporate communications for Cleveland-Cliffs, told CBC News in an emailed statement that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.
"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in an email. "We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."
At a news conference in Vancouver Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the Stelco situation, saying his thoughts were with the "workers and their families who have been betrayed by the company."
He did not directly answer when a reporter asked if Ottawa was considering legal action over the company appearing to break its employment commitment.
Cleveland-Cliffs "has legal obligations for employment," Carney said, adding that the government intends to use "all powers that we have and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law."
Stelco 'betrayed' Ontario workers with layoffs, Carney says
Carney added that U.S. tariffs caused the situation, noting that Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has praised them. In 2024, Goncalves told CBC Hamilton that tariffs on imports into the U.S. were "a great move."
Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said Monday the city had been working with the federal and provincial governments in response to the announcement.
"The fight is not over," Horwath told CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.
She said she believes Cleveland-Cliffs is not living up to commitments made to workers and that she has asked city staff to review commitments made during the company's restructuring process.
"We're going to fight tooth and nail to have them basically live up to their commitments and protect these jobs," she said.
Hamilton steelworkers union, business leaders warn of harder times ahead as Ford promises tariff relief
Karina Gould, the Liberal MP for nearby Burlington, called the decision "devastating news" for Hamilton and said the federal government is prepared to provide support to maintain operations and protect jobs.
"This is a very difficult time," Gould said.
Hamilton mayoral candidate Keanin Loomis, who is the president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, also called the announcement "devastating."
"Steel jobs have supported generations of Hamilton families and remain vital to our local economy," Loomis said in a statement on social media.
The impact of tariffs has been a discussion topic on the municipal election campaign trail, with several candidates sharing proposals on how to respond to trade uncertainty.
Hamilton mayor announces 7-point tariff-response plan
For Watt, the announcement represents another difficult moment for a city where steel means so much.
"My grandfather, my dad, my uncles, they all worked at Stelco," she said. "My husband and my brother are there, and this is going to have a huge impact."

articles.title_orig: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
articles.title_zh: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
articles.content_orig:
Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.
This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.
Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.
He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.
Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”
Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem . Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.
Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof . The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.
Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter .
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.
Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.
Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.
His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July . He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.title_zh: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month.
Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September.
South Korea said on Tuesday that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, were "highly likely" from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what it said was a violation of a decades-old armistice.
North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation".
Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea.
Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making."
South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border.
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War.
That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5mi) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas.
In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ.
In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied.
Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now.
Ties between Pyongyang and Seoul have only deteriorated since 2015, raising the risk of friction when such incidents happen.
Christopher Green, a senior consultant with Crisis Group, tells the BBC that "The North Koreans have been wilfully attempting to harden the border [and] eliminate inter-Korean relations".
As a result, he adds, the two Koreas no longer have the "same low-level communication" that they shared in 2015.
"Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he says.
The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms".
"UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said.

Constitutional law attorney Jonathan Turley joins ‘America’s Newsroom’ to break down the legal battle over New York City’s controversial pied-à-terre tax after a judge blocked its implementation.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday quickly appealed a judge’s decision to cancel previously mailed notices for his second-home tax, triggering an automatic stay of the ruling.
"The auto stay allows the city to continue, as we have been, with the implementation of the pied-a-terre surcharge and puts the lower court’s order on pause," a city official said.
Just hours earlier, Judge Wayne Ozzi found that the city failed to follow required procedures before mailing the notices, which he described as "arbitrary and capricious, affected by errors of law, and in violation of the recipients’ due process rights," according to the ruling.
Despite the ruling, Ozzi noted that the policy itself could still survive. He said the city can still apply the tax by removing the current list of taxed properties from its website and posting a corrected list after following the proper procedures.
MAMDANI’S LUXURY-HOME TAX ROLLOUT DERAILED FOR NOW AS JUDGE DELIVERS WIN TO NYC HOMEOWNERS OVER MASSIVE LIST
A spokesperson for Mamdani defended the tax as a "basic principle of fairness" for funding city services. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images/File)
New notices must then be mailed in compliance with the law.
Tuesday's decision served as a legal speed bump for Mamdani as he approaches nearly a year since he was elected New York City mayor and is among a handful of other legal challenges he faces as he attempts to implement government-first approaches to promises to bring down costs of living, expand housing and increase public transportation.
In addition to his second-home tax, Mamdani has also faced legal pushback on his rent freeze plan, which landlords have characterized as overly punitive, his state-sponsored grocery store plan, which has sparked challenges from the National Supermarket Association and what they see as unfair competition and challenges to specialized high school admissions that some parents believe unfairly discriminates against Asian-American enrollees.
Mamdani announced the second-home tax back in April.
In its original form, it was designed to levy an annual surcharge on one to three family homes, condominiums and co-ops valued at above $5 million. It also only applied to owners who also had additional property outside of New York City.
MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'
Brownstone apartments in Manhattan, N.Y., July 6, 2024. A judge ruled Tuesday that previously mailed notices for Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s luxury second-home tax must be canceled. (Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
"Thanks to the support of Governor Hochul, we are one step closer to balancing our budget by taxing the ultra-wealthy and global elites with a pied-à-terre tax — the first of its kind in our state. Alongside the governor, our administration is fighting every day to make sure we address this fiscal deficit fairly, where the wealthy contribute what they owe and our budget reflects our commitment to the working New Yorkers being priced out of our city," Mamdani said in a press release at the time.
Asked about the plan after Tuesday's decision, representatives for Mamdani said the mayor would stand by his plan.
Matt Rauschenbach, a spokesperson for the mayor, defended the tax rollout, arguing that the pied-à-terre surcharge is a "basic principle of fairness" that supports a city he said should not be a "tax haven for the wealthy few."
"If you can afford a luxury second home in New York City, you can afford to pay your fair share for the schools, streets and parks that make this city work," Rauschenbach said.
"Our administration is fighting every day to deliver for working New Yorkers. The ultra-wealthy are fighting in court to avoid paying their fair share. They have filed lawsuit after lawsuit to protect their privilege, and we will not back down.

articles.title_zh: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
articles.content_orig:
Trump was speaking at the launch of America.gov, an AI-powered web portal for US government services
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.
At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation".
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI.
A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order , external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".
He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".
Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.
Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.
Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.
In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."
He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."
Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.
Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.
However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.
Speaking to broadcasters after Burnham's speech, Reform leader Nigel Farage said he was open to debating a potential change to the system "at some point" but other issues were "far more urgent".
He added: "Is this an absolute priority for the general election after the next one? I don't believe that it is."
Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.
Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.
At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.
Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.
Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system .

articles.title_orig: Spain protests: Evicted 87-year-old woman to return to Madrid home
articles.title_zh: Spain protests: Evicted 87-year-old woman to return to Madrid home
articles.content_orig:
Large protests have erupted in Spain over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman who is set to return to her Madrid home, her representatives said.
The lawyer representing Maria del Carmen Abascal, known across Spain as Maricarmen, said on Tuesday that the real estate firm offered to reduce her rent back to its pre-dispute rate.
Under the deal, her monthly payments would be capped at about $570 for the next eight years, taking up roughly 30 percent of her pension.
This is the latest development in an ongoing saga that started with her eviction last week.
Maricarmen became the face of Spain’s deepening housing crisis after an international investment fund bought her building and hiked her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.
Madrid’s tenants’ union organised protests and encampments in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, drawing tens of thousands of demonstrators before spreading to dozens of other cities.
Upon the announcement of the landlord’s offer, the union celebrated what it described as a “historic win” in a post on X.
The government of Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez responded to the outcry by presenting a package of measures scheduled for a parliamentary vote this Friday.
The proposal most likely to secure approval extends expired tenant safeguards through 2030, shielding vulnerable residents like Abascal from eviction over that period.
The package falls short of the protesters’ demands and is likely to face opposition from conservative parties more sympathetic to landlords’ interests.
According to Spain’s central bank, the country is roughly 755,000 homes short of demand, a gap that could widen to a million units by 2028.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.content_orig:
Goldman Sachs is on top of Wall Street right now, advising on more than $1 trillion in merger deals and generating more than $12 billion in equities revenue in the first six months of the year alone.
Those records make it all the more striking that Goldman's board has reportedly discussed replacing CEO David Solomon, 64, with president John Waldron, 57, as early as next year.
The succession plan, which would elevate Solomon to executive chairman, could be voted on by the bank's board in coming months, The Wall Street Journal reported late Monday.
The transition would be one of the "smoother and more deliberate" leadership handovers seen on Wall Street, Wells Fargo banking analyst Mike Mayo wrote Monday.
But there's a key risk facing Goldman: Solomon may not be ready to give up his seat, and Waldron may not be willing to wait for it indefinitely.
Solomon has gotten Goldman back on track after an ill-fated foray into consumer banking earlier in his tenure. With help from a deals rebound powered by the Trump administration and the artificial intelligence boom, Goldman is once again a clean story for investors: It's the top pure-play investment bank.
"It's just very hard for a person like that to decide they are really going to retire," said retired University of Delaware law professor Charles Elson . "Being 65 years old today is like being 55 was 30 years ago."
Elson also noted that Solomon is chairman of Goldman's board and holds outsized influence over the body, making it hard for him to be forced out.
Goldman spokesman Tony Fratto said there is "no definitive timeline for succession" at the bank. Bank boards often discuss succession planning over the near, medium and longer term.
Another expert in CEO succession, Yale School of Management's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, said it would be bad governance if Goldman's board was trying to "drive out a high performing CEO like David Solomon."
Under Solomon, who took over as CEO in 2018, Goldman shares are up more than 300%, the second-best performance versus the KBW Bank Index , according to Mayo. Only JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon , who has led his firm for nearly 21 years, has done better.
That leaves Goldman in something of a bind: Even if Solomon is planning on leaving in a year, he has little incentive to say so. Doing so would make him a lame duck with less influence inside the bank, according to Elson.
But if Solomon decides he wants to remain CEO amid an AI boom that he believes is in its early innings, Waldron may tire of waiting for the crown.
After all, Waldron, Goldman's president and chief operating officer, had reportedly been in discussions for leadership roles at alternative asset managers Apollo and Carlyle .
To keep him, Goldman gave Waldron an $80 million retention package that lasts through 2030. Even then, a deep-pocketed suitor could make a play for Waldron, said Elson.
"There will always be tension in a set up like that," Elson said. "It's like Prince Charles waiting for his mother to die. You can't set your own priorities, because there's someone else in charge."

articles.title_orig: Pages, Keynote, Numbers, and Pixelmator Pro just got new features
articles.title_zh: Pages, Keynote, Numbers, and Pixelmator Pro just got new features
articles.content_orig:
Today alongside a big update to Final Cut Camera, Apple announced that it’s rolling out updated versions of Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, and Freeform. Here’s what’s new.
Apple has announced new features coming to its popular iWork suite today—Pages, Keynote, and Numbers—alongside improvements for Pixelmator Pro and Freeform.
Some additions are exclusive to Apple Creator Studio, but select features will be available for all users. Here’s everything new, per Apple Newsroom :
Apple says that today’s updates bring support for asking Siri questions about Pages, Keynote, or Numbers and get answers. It’s unclear if Siri AI is required or not, but that’s likely. The updates also enable “the ability to request access to a shared presentation, document, or spreadsheet.” This makes collaboration easier, as the file owner no longer needs to initiate file sharing.
Pages for Mac has a new Screen View, which “optimizes content for reading and focused writing.” And Numbers gets “new trigonometry, statistics, and logic functions for solving complex problems in a spreadsheet.”
Additionally, for Apple Creator Studio subscribers there are new templates and themes available across all three iWork apps. And in Keynote, intelligent slide generation will automatically make images that are tailored to a given presentation.
Pixelmator Pro on iPad adds Select and Mask tools that were previously Mac-exclusive. And both Mac and iPad apps gain two template collections for sports and action-centric projects, plus new templates for “launching a new creative idea, business, or product.”
And if you're wondering if the Pixelmator Pro stand alone app received an update? The answer is no (at least not yet). Current version 3.8 has not been updated for about 5 months.
Additionally, there’s a new Podcasts category for creating cover artwork that’s sized to fit well on major podcast platforms.
Freeform gains several highly requested features. Boards now automatically adapt to Dark Mode, and folders let users organize boards into collections and invite others to collaborate. Writing Tools with Apple Intelligence can rewrite, proofread, and summarize handwritten notes; users can also request access to collaborate on shared files, or automate adding content using Shortcuts. Freeform becomes even more powerful in visionOS 27, letting users pull multiple items from a board — including images, videos, sticky notes, shapes, and 3D models — into their space, and view 3D models together as a group.

articles.title_orig: Meta Plans VR Glasses Strap Accessory for Active VR Gaming
articles.title_zh: Meta Plans VR Glasses Strap Accessory for Active VR Gaming
articles.content_orig:
Meta VR Glasses can play all of the same games you might on Quest, whether it be through integrated hand-tracking or by pairing optional Touch Plus controllers. But if you’re planning on getting active, Meta says they’ll be selling an accessory for that.
We haven’t seen any images yet, however at Connect 2026 last week the company not only announced Meta VR Glasses, which are coming in Spring 2027 for $1,300, but also the answer to the question of how users will be able to play active VR games.
The solution: a cinching strap that connects the tips of both of the glasses’ temple arms together, more securely fastening it to the user’s head, i.e. not an entirely new strap system like is often the case with Quest.
As it was described to me, it will physically connect to the temple arms, the tips of which actually can be detached for more modularity.
And with a glasses form factor, it needs it. During my hands-on with VR Glasses at Connect , it did feel fairly solid on its own, with no nose-slipping or ear-clipping as some glasses-type headsets are wont to do.
Anything that requires fast head or body movement, or looking down for extended amounts of time though, and you’d probably want a good way of keeping the glasses snug, not only so they don’t fly off your head, but also to keep their relatively narrow sweet spot in place.
Thus far, the only other extras mentioned to me include a light blocker accessory that magnetically attaches to the glasses for greater immersion and prescription lenses from Zenni Optical.
I expect we’ll see those and more accessories closer to its launch next year, and also hopefully learn whether the strap will be a paid add-on, or it will come in the box.
